content: 1. A diagnosis of HIV-positive status should be confirmed only after three sequential reactive tests. 2. If the result of Assay 1 is reactive but Assay 2 is non-reactive, the final result should be considered HIV-negative. 3. However, if Assay 1 is a fourth-generation antibody/antigen (Ab/Ag) test and Assay 2 is an antibody-only test, the result is inconclusive, and the individual should be retested after 14 days. 4. For cases where Assay 1 and Assay 2 are reactive but Assay 3 is non-reactive, the result is also inconclusive, and the individual should return for retesting in 14 days. 5. Oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) containing tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) should be offered as an additional prevention option for individuals at substantial risk of HIV infection as part of a combination prevention strategy. This is a strong recommendation based on high-quality evidence. 6. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for HIV is effective with a two-drug regimen, but a three-drug regimen is preferred. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 7. For adults and adolescents, lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) or atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r) is recommended as the preferred third drug in PEP regimens. Where available, raltegravir (RAL), darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r), or efavirenz (EFV) can be considered as alternative options. 8. For children aged ≤10 years, zidovudine (AZT) + lamivudine (3TC) is the preferred backbone regimen for PEP. Alternatives include abacavir (ABC) + 3TC or TDF + 3TC (or emtricitabine [FTC]). LPV/r is the preferred third drug for children under 10 years of age. 9. A full 28-day prescription of antiretroviral drugs should be provided for PEP following an initial risk assessment. Enhanced adherence counseling is suggested for all individuals initiating PEP. 10. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated in all adults living with HIV, regardless of WHO clinical stage or CD4 cell count. Priority should be given to adults with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) or CD4 counts ≤350 cells/mm³. 11. ART should be initiated in all pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count, and continued lifelong. 12. ART should be initiated in all adolescents (10–19 years old) living with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count. Priority should be given to those with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease or CD4 counts ≤350 cells/mm³. 13. ART should be initiated in all children living with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count. Infants diagnosed in the first year of life should start ART immediately. Children aged 1–10 years should also start ART, with priority given to those under 2 years of age or with advanced disease. 14. ART should be started in all individuals with active tuberculosis (TB) and HIV, regardless of CD4 count. TB treatment should be initiated first, followed by ART as soon as possible within the first 8 weeks of TB treatment. For individuals with CD4 counts <50 cells/mm³, ART should be started within the first 2 weeks of TB treatment. 15. First-line ART for adults should consist of two nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) plus either a non-nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) or an integrase inhibitor (INSTI). The preferred regimen is TDF + 3TC (or FTC) + EFV as a fixed-dose combination. 16. Fixed-dose combinations and once-daily regimens are preferred for ART. Countries should discontinue the use of stavudine (d4T) in first-line regimens due to its metabolic toxicities. 17. For children aged 3–10 years, the preferred NRTI backbone is ABC + 3TC. Alternatives include AZT or TDF + 3TC (or FTC). EFV is the preferred NNRTI for children aged 3 years and older. 18. For children younger than 3 years, the preferred NRTI backbone is ABC or AZT + 3TC. An LPV/r-based regimen should be used as first-line ART for all children under 3 years of age, regardless of NNRTI exposure. 19. Infants born to mothers with HIV who are at high risk of acquiring HIV should receive dual prophylaxis with AZT (twice daily) and NVP (once daily) for the first 6 weeks of life, regardless of feeding method. 20. Breastfed infants at high risk of HIV acquisition should continue prophylaxis for an additional 6 weeks (total of 12 weeks) using either AZT + NVP or NVP alone. 21. Infants of mothers receiving ART and breastfeeding should receive 6 weeks of daily NVP prophylaxis. If replacement feeding is used, infants should receive 4–6 weeks of daily NVP or twice-daily AZT. 22. National health authorities should decide whether to counsel and support HIV-infected mothers to breastfeed with ARV interventions or to avoid breastfeeding entirely. In settings promoting breastfeeding, mothers should exclusively breastfeed for the first 6 months, introduce complementary foods thereafter, and continue breastfeeding for 12 months. 23. Routine viral load monitoring should be conducted at 6 months, 12 months, and annually thereafter for patients stable on ART. CD4 monitoring can be stopped in individuals who are stable on ART and virally suppressed. 24. Viral load is the preferred method for diagnosing and confirming treatment failure. Virologic failure is defined as a persistently detectable viral load >1,000 copies/mL after at least 6 months on a new ART regimen, with adherence support provided. 25. Second-line ART for adults and adolescents should consist of two NRTIs plus a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor (PI). After failure on a TDF + 3TC (or FTC)-based first-line regimen, AZT + 3TC should be used as the NRTI backbone in second-line regimens.
